The board is the feature herddash is measured by: a notification center with one box per agent showing status, owning account and time waiting, sorted longest-waiting first; read-only, no terminal, no chat, no pane control. The recorder engine (subscribe, persist transitions, attribute, read-only API, event stream) is what makes the board trustworthy and feeds future surfaces. Corrects ADR-0001's consequence that the board is secondary; to be recorded as ADR-0003.

Why: The operator's daily value is glancing at the board in another window all day; a PRD that calls it secondary would produce epics that treat it as secondary, the success metric (noticing a waiting agent sooner than the toast) is a board metric, and the differentiator the operator believes in is restraint, a notification center rather than a browser client, which can only be defended if the board is the product being restrained.

Story 1.7 resync design (spec-1-7): resync is a named engine operation triggered by any status-stream health signal, a rejected/failed status subscribe, or a snapshot showing a tracked Agent without a subscription. One resync runs at a time, a trigger during one causes exactly one more, and resyncs start at least resyncMinInterval (default 5 s) apart. A reconcile timer requests a snapshot every reconcileInterval (default 60 s). Lifecycle-stream signals keep Story 1.6's reconnect, whose Reconnected report is the marker.

Why: AD-11 requires a single resync guard and minimum interval in the engine, and FR-7 requires every gap to be announced. Funnelling the per-pane recovery paths through one guarded operation serialises a lost-events condition that drops many pane connections, and makes the persistent-rejection loop cost one subscribe per interval. The lifecycle stream already has a reconnect that resubscribes, snapshots and replaces state.

Story 2.2 recording (spec-2-2): the engine writes every Transition through store.Append when it observes it, including an Agent's first sight as a Transition with no previous Status (snapshot provenance from apply, live from a status event). It writes a daemon_start resync marker at Run start. The epoch and pane→terminal_id map persist in a mutable server_state table (migration 0002), upserted after a snapshot changes them. At start the engine loads them and runs Story 1.6's epoch rule on the first snapshot. History reads order by observed_at then id (the binding spine rule); the epic AC's "herdr's order" wording is superseded by the Story 1.3 finding. A failed write is logged, never fatal.

Why: ADR-0005 and AD-4 make the record append-only, but the epoch is engine state, not the record. Without persisting it, a Daemon restart restarts at epoch 1 and splices a new herdr instance's Agents onto old history (AD-3 hazard 3). Recording first sight makes the record hold every Agent's current Status (FR-7 consequence 2). Story 2.4 owns deciding how the fold treats a first-sight row whose Status equals the last stored one.

Story 2.4 Waiting Time (spec-2-4): core.ClassOf maps blocked→needs_you, done→finished, idle→finished if the Agent was ever working (else working), working→working, unknown/none→unknown. core.Fold over an Agent's ordered Transitions gives Status, Class, Since (the ObservedAt of the Transition where the current class began; done→idle keeps it), SinceProvenance and EverWorking. At first sight with a store, it reads History(key): if the last stored Status equals the one seen, it writes no row and keeps the fold (exact survives a Daemon restart); if they differ, it records a Transition whose previous Status is the stored one. serve prints class= and waiting= (≥ for a lower bound).

text: Store calls in herddash must not run under a context that shutdown cancels. When a transaction's context is cancelled, database/sql rolls it back in a background goroutine, and DB.Close does not wait for that connection. So right after Store.Close returns, SQLite's lock can still be held, and the next store.Open gets SQLITE_BUSY. This was seen once on Linux CI in TestServeTwice (PR #30) and did not reproduce on macOS. The engine therefore passes context.WithoutCancel(runCtx) to Sweep and History. The cause is inferred from database/sql's semantics, not proven.

Story 2.6 import (spec-2-6): `herddash import-plugin-log <file> --herdr-0.9.2-since <date>` parses the agent-webhook hook.log. It handles two forms (`posted <status> for <pane> -> <code>`, and `would have sent {json}` with an optional profile), with local-time stamps. Each entry becomes a backfill Transition under epoch 0, with NULL previous Status, state_change_seq and herdr version. The import_key is a SHA-256 of host, server and the raw line, plus the occurrence index. `done` entries before local midnight of the given date are flagged possibly spurious. On a Host that never ran 0.9.2+ (this machine's server is 0.8.2), pass a date after the last entry. Entries older than Retention are skipped. Rows are written by store.AppendBackfill: the same INSERT as Append, in one transaction, skipping existing import keys. Spine AD-13 is amended to say so.

Why: FR-9a and AD-13. Host and Server are in the key so a mis-keyed first import can be corrected by re-running with the right flags. A batch transaction makes the import all-or-nothing and fast. It shares the single INSERT statement, so the rows cannot differ in shape from the engine's.

Story 7.2 (R8): the Daemon rotates its own herddash.log by size, at 10 MiB, keeping two earlier files (herddash.log.1, .2; about 30 MiB at most), all 0600. The writer lives in cmd/herddash and uses only the standard library. The limit and count are fixed tunables, not config keys. herddash.stderr.log (launchd) and the journal (systemd) are not rotated by herddash. A failed rotation keeps writing to the open file and reports once to stderr.

Why: Observed growth is about 23 KB/day (212 KB in 9 days), so 10 MiB is about a year per file. Size rotation inside the binary needs no dependency, no ADR (not a structural change), and no deployment change on either OS.
